findings.proposedIrEvidence: conditions: [] ; exceptions: [] ; capacityExpression only encodes 'in an aggregate amount equal to $25,000,000 since the Closing Date' (see provenance excerpts, which quote only the amount/duration language)
findings.sourceEvidence: (c) redemptions of Capital Stock in connection with a rights plan adopted by the Board of Directors of the Parent Borrower in an aggregate amount equal to $25,000,000 since the Closing Date;
findings.verifierReasoning: The proposed IR represents clause (c) as a permission to make $25,000,000 of Capital Stock redemptions, cumulative since the Closing Date, with no qualifying condition at all. The source, however, makes the permission expressly conditional on the redemptions being 'in connection with a rights plan adopted by the Board of Directors of the Parent Borrower.' That phrase is an independently operative eligibility requirement defining the scope of the exception: it is not merely descriptive color, it is what ties the basket to a specific transaction type (a poison-pill/rights plan redemption). The proposed IR drops this requirement entirely (conditions empty, exceptions empty, and the capacity provenance excerpts quote only the amount and duration). The test for discrepancy: construct a transaction in which the Parent Borrower makes $25,000,000 of redemptions of its Capital Stock since the Closing Date that are NOT in connection with any board-adopted rights plan. Under the real source, clause (c) does not permit those redemptions (they would fall back to the general Restricted Payments prohibition, potentially failing to qualify under any other clause). Under the proposed IR as written, such a $25,000,000 redemption would appear fully permitted. The two readings yield different compliance conclusions, so this is a genuine discrepancy. A competent reviewer evaluating available capacity under (c) would alter their conclusion (a $25M unrestricted redemption capacity vs. a $25M capacity usable only for rights-plan-connected redemptions) — material. The claim of COMPLETE sufficiency is therefore over-broad.
